entities.label: Text
entities.summary: The Tanakh, also known as the Hebrew Bible or the Torah, is a foundational text in Judaism, comprising the core scriptures for the Jewish faith. Written primarily in Hebrew with some Aramaic, it was compiled over several centuries, with the earliest texts dating back to around 800 BCE. The Tanakh contains 24 books, including the Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings), which together narrate the creation of the world, the history of the Israelites, and the prophetic messages. Its significance extends beyond Judaism, influencing Western literature, art, and philosophy, and shaping the moral and ethical frameworks of many societies. The Tanakh's impact can be seen in the works of Aristotle, Plato, and the Christian New Testament, as well as in the development of Western law, literature, and art. Its legacy continues to inspire Jewish communities worldwide, as well as broader cultural and religious discussions, with ongoing debates about its interpretation and relevance in modern times. The Tanakh's significance is reflected in its enduring influence on Jewish identity, as well as its role in shaping Western cultural heritage.
